newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria swept by strikes on 24th day of protests.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria swept by strikes on 24th day of protests.

text.p: Bulgaria, already economically devastated, was hit by widespread anti-government strikes on Wednesday as workers joined students and opposition parties in demanding elections to pull the Balkan country from crisis.
Teachers, transport workers, miners, hospital staff and factory workers around Bulgaria stopped work during the day for an hour to back anti-government protests, state radio said.
Train services in the Black Sea Bourgas region and in the second city of Plovdiv were halted. The highway to the Danube port of Rousse was blocked. Traffic stretched for kilometres.
Many plants stopped work and opposition party supporters blocked the Bulgaria-Greece highway for an hour, Bulgarian state radio said.
The workers were heeding a call by three independent trade unions to back 24 days of protests against the policies of the ruling ex-communist Socialists and to demand elections.
Underscoring the depth of the crisis, President Petar Stoyanov said in Brussels that Bulgaria may have to default on its debt repayments this year unless it receives badly needed financial help.

"Bulgaria is due to make payments on its external debt later this year which will face our financial system with a final collapse...a default and a moratorium on our payments is not out of the question," he told NATO ambassadors.

Stoyanov, a pro-market liberal who took office last week, was stating what many Bulgarians and foreign bankers have known for some time but he was the first official to state it publicly. Bulgaria's foreign debt is about $10 billion.

Under the constitution, Stoyanov had to give the Socialists a mandate to form a new government before he left. But he urged them to return it, join the opposition in adopting badly needed economic reforms and holding elections.

The Socialists have overseen a caretaker government since December 21 when prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned after Stoyanov scored a landslide election win. The victory was seen as public repudiation of Socialist economic policies.
Organisations such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have withheld credit to Bulgaria, saying the Socialists failed to embrace reform after their election in December 1994.
The IMF is withholding a $115 million credit, saying that it wants to see action on closing loss-making state companies and privatisation.
Students and the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) have staged colourful protests since January 6 to pressure the government to hold early elections.
State taxis joined in the festivities on Wednesday, with hundreds of Russian-made Lada cabs racing through central Sofia hooting horns and waving the blue UDF flag.
Students held a candle-light parade and planned a spoof Miss Protest and Mr Vagabond contest -- critics have refered to the youthful protesters as "mere vagabonds".

Aside from student gaiety, the public's mood has been grim with the lev in freefall and inflation soaring. The main branch of the State Savings Bank was crammed with depositors trying to withdraw money which was losing its value by the hour.

"I am fed up with all this chaos," said Mikhail Shopov. "I do not care that the dollar is at 1,500 now. Last week, when I could buy dollars at 800-900, I decided to wait for some time and I was wrong."
Interior minister Nikolai Dobrev, who will try to form a new government over the next week, appears determined to keep the Socialists in power and to buy time before an election.

"Nikolai Dobrev is desperately trying to invite the opposition for talks on formation of a coalition government but we will not accept any proposal," UDF leader Ivan Kostov told the daily opposition rally.

The UDF said it would suspend its boycott of parliament to try to stop Dobrev from winning approval for his cabinet. But the Socialists have an absolute majority and the UDF is pinning its hopes on defections from Socialist party ranks.
